{{Short description|Mathematical formula for viscous fluid}}
{{one source |date=April 2024}}
[[File:RankineVortex.svg|thumb|upright=1.3|Velocity distribution in a Rankine vortex.]]
[[File:Rankine vortex animation.gif|thumb|Animation of a Rankine vortex. Free-floating test particles reveal the velocity and vorticity pattern.]]
The '''Rankine vortex''' is a simple mathematical model of a [[vortex]] in a [[Viscosity|viscous]] fluid. It is named after its discoverer, [[William John Macquorn Rankine]].

The vortices observed in nature are usually modelled with an [[Potential flow#Examples of two-dimensional flows#Line vortex|irrotational]] (potential or free) vortex. However, in a potential vortex, the velocity becomes infinite at the vortex center. In reality, very close to the origin, the motion resembles a solid body rotation. The Rankine vortex model assumes a solid-body rotation inside a cylinder of radius <math>a</math> and a potential vortex outside the cylinder. The radius <math>a</math> is referred to as the vortex-core radius. The velocity components <math>(v_r,v_\theta,v_z)</math> of the Rankine vortex, expressed in terms of the cylindrical-coordinate system <math>(r,\theta,z)</math> are given by<ref>{{cite book
  | title = Elementary Fluid Dynamics
  | author = D. J. Acheson
  | publisher = [[Oxford University Press]]
  | year = 1990
  | isbn = 0-19-859679-0
  }}</ref>

:<math>v_r=0,\quad v_\theta(r) = \frac{\Gamma}{2\pi}\begin{cases}  r/a^2 & r \le a, \\ 1/ r & r > a \end{cases}, \quad v_z = 0</math>

where <math>\Gamma</math> is the [[Circulation (fluid dynamics)|circulation strength]] of the Rankine vortex. Since solid-body rotation is characterized by an azimuthal velocity <math>\Omega r</math>, where <math>\Omega</math> is the constant [[angular velocity]], the parameter <math>\Omega =\Gamma/(2\pi a^2)</math> can also be used to characterize the vortex.

The [[vorticity]] field <math>(\omega_r,\omega_\theta,\omega_z)</math> associated with the Rankine vortex is

:<math>\omega_r=0,\quad \omega_\theta=0, \quad \omega_z = \begin{cases}  2\Omega & r \le a, \\ 0 & r > a \end{cases}.</math>

At all points inside the core of the Rankine vortex, the vorticity is uniform at twice the angular velocity of the core; whereas vorticity is zero at all points outside the core because the flow there is irrotational.

In reality, vortex cores are not always circular; and vorticity is not exactly uniform throughout the vortex core.
